Unless they are all 0, in which case this\n            // is the indefinite form.\n            0x80 => Ok(Length::Indefinite),\n            0x81 => {\n                let len = source.take_u8()? as usize;\n                if mode.is_ber() || len > 127 {\n                    Ok(Length::Definite(len))\n                }\n                else {\n                    Err(source.content_err(\"invalid length\"))\n                }\n            }\n            0x82 => {\n                let len =\n                    (source.take_u8()? as usize) << 8 |\n                    (source.take_u8()? as usize);\n                if mode.is_ber() || len > 255 {\n                    Ok(Length::Definite(len))\n                }\n                else {\n                    Err(source.content_err(\"invalid length\"))\n                }\n            }\n            0x83 => {\n                let len =\n                    (source.take_u8()? as usize) << 16 |\n                    (source.take_u8()? as usize) << 8 |\n                    (source.take_u8()? as usize);\n                if mode.is_ber() || len > 0xFFFF {\n                    Ok(Length::Definite(len))\n                }\n                else {\n                    Err(source.content_err(\"invalid length\"))\n                }\n            }\n            0x84 => {\n                let len =\n                    (source.take_u8()? as usize) << 24 |\n                    (source.take_u8()? as usize) << 16 |\n                    (source.take_u8()? as usize) << 8 |\n                    (source.take_u8()? as usize);\n                if mode.is_ber() || len > 0x00FF_FFFF {\n                    Ok(Length::Definite(len))\n                }\n                else {\n                    Err(source.content_err(\"invalid length\"))\n                }\n            }\n            _ => {\n                // We only implement up to two length bytes for now.\n                Err(source.content_err(\n                    \"lengths over 4 bytes not implemented\"\n                ))\n            }\n        }\n    }"

For example, arrays (`[T]`) implement\n    /// [`IntoIterator`], and so can be passed to `zip()` directly:\n    ///\n    /// ```\n    /// let a1 = [1, 2, 3];\n    /// let a2 = [4, 5, 6];\n    ///\n    /// let mut iter = a1.into_iter().zip(a2);\n    ///\n    /// assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some((1, 4)));\n    /// assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some((2, 5)));\n    /// assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some((3, 6)));\n    /// assert_eq!(iter.next(), None);\n    /// ```\n    ///\n    /// `zip()` is often used to zip an infinite iterator to a finite one.\n    /// This works because the finite iterator will eventually return [`None`],\n    /// ending the zipper. Zipping with `(0..)` can look a lot like [`enumerate`]:\n    ///\n    /// ```\n    /// let enumerate: Vec<_> = \"foo\".chars().enumerate().collect();\n    ///\n    /// let zipper: Vec<_> = (0..).zip(\"foo\".chars()).collect();\n    ///\n    /// assert_eq!((0, 'f'), enumerate[0]);\n    /// assert_eq!((0, 'f'), zipper[0]);\n    ///\n    /// assert_eq!((1, 'o'), enumerate[1]);\n    /// assert_eq!((1, 'o'), zipper[1]);\n    ///\n    /// assert_eq!((2, 'o'), enumerate[2]);\n    /// assert_eq!((2, 'o'), zipper[2]);\n    /// ```\n    ///\n    /// If both iterators have roughly equivalent syntax, it may be more readable to use [`zip`]:\n    ///\n    /// ```\n    /// use std::iter::zip;\n    ///\n    /// let a = [1, 2, 3];\n    /// let b = [2, 3, 4];\n    ///\n    /// let mut zipped = zip(\n    ///     a.into_iter().map(|x| x * 2).skip(1),\n    ///     b.into_iter().map(|x| x * 2).skip(1),\n    /// );\n    ///\n    /// assert_eq!(zipped.next(), Some((4, 6)));\n    /// assert_eq!(zipped.next(), Some((6, 8)));\n    /// assert_eq!(zipped.next(), None);\n    /// ```\n    ///\n    /// compared to:\n    ///\n    /// ```\n    /// # let a = [1, 2, 3];\n    /// # let b = [2, 3, 4];\n    /// #\n    /// let mut zipped = a\n    ///     .into_iter()\n    ///     .map(|x| x * 2)\n    ///     .skip(1)\n    ///     .zip(b.into_iter().map(|x| x * 2).skip(1));\n    /// #\n    /// # assert_eq!(zipped.next(), Some((4, 6)));\n    /// # assert_eq!(zipped.next(), Some((6, 8)));\n    /// # assert_eq!(zipped.next(), None);\n    /// ```\n    ///\n    /// [`enumerate`]: Iterator::enumerate\n    /// [`next`]: Iterator::next\n    /// [`zip`]: crate::iter::zip\n    #[inline]\n    #[stable(feature = \"rust1\", since = \"1.0.0\")]\n    fn zip<U>(self, other: U) -> Zip<Self, U::IntoIter>\n    where\n        Self: Sized,\n        U: IntoIterator,\n    {\n        Zip::new(self, other.into_iter())\n    }"

For example, arrays (`[T]`) implement\n    /// [`IntoIterator`], and so can be passed to `zip()` directly:\n    ///\n    /// ```\n    /// let a1 = [1, 2, 3];\n    /// let a2 = [4, 5, 6];\n    ///\n    /// let mut iter = a1.into_iter().zip(a2);\n    ///\n    /// assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some((1, 4)));\n    /// assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some((2, 5)));\n    /// assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some((3, 6)));\n    /// assert_eq!(iter.next(), None);\n    /// ```\n    ///\n    /// `zip()` is often used to zip an infinite iterator to a finite one.\n    /// This works because the finite iterator will eventually return [`None`],\n    /// ending the zipper. Zipping with `(0..)` can look a lot like [`enumerate`]:\n    ///\n    /// ```\n    /// let enumerate: Vec<_> = \"foo\".chars().enumerate().collect();\n    ///\n    /// let zipper: Vec<_> = (0..).zip(\"foo\".chars()).collect();\n    ///\n    /// assert_eq!((0, 'f'), enumerate[0]);\n    /// assert_eq!((0, 'f'), zipper[0]);\n    ///\n    /// assert_eq!((1, 'o'), enumerate[1]);\n    /// assert_eq!((1, 'o'), zipper[1]);\n    ///\n    /// assert_eq!((2, 'o'), enumerate[2]);\n    /// assert_eq!((2, 'o'), zipper[2]);\n    /// ```\n    ///\n    /// If both iterators have roughly equivalent syntax, it may be more readable to use [`zip`]:\n    ///\n    /// ```\n    /// use std::iter::zip;\n    ///\n    /// let a = [1, 2, 3];\n    /// let b = [2, 3, 4];\n    ///\n    /// let mut zipped = zip(\n    ///     a.into_iter().map(|x| x * 2).skip(1),\n    ///     b.into_iter().map(|x| x * 2).skip(1),\n    /// );\n    ///\n    /// assert_eq!(zipped.next(), Some((4, 6)));\n    /// assert_eq!(zipped.next(), Some((6, 8)));\n    /// assert_eq!(zipped.next(), None);\n    /// ```\n    ///\n    /// compared to:\n    ///\n    /// ```\n    /// # let a = [1, 2, 3];\n    /// # let b = [2, 3, 4];\n    /// #\n    /// let mut zipped = a\n    ///     .into_iter()\n    ///     .map(|x| x * 2)\n    ///     .skip(1)\n    ///     .zip(b.into_iter().map(|x| x * 2).skip(1));\n    /// #\n    /// # assert_eq!(zipped.next(), Some((4, 6)));\n    /// # assert_eq!(zipped.next(), Some((6, 8)));\n    /// # assert_eq!(zipped.next(), None);\n    /// ```\n    ///\n    /// [`enumerate`]: Iterator::enumerate\n    /// [`next`]: Iterator::next\n    /// [`zip`]: crate::iter::zip\n    #[inline]\n    #[stable(feature = \"rust1\", since = \"1.0.0\")]\n    fn zip<U>(self, other: U) -> Zip<Self, U::IntoIter>\n    where\n        Self: Sized,\n        U: IntoIterator,\n    {\n        Zip::new(self, other.into_iter())\n    }"

If the vector's length would exceed its\n    /// capacity after the push, *O*(*capacity*) time is taken to copy the\n    /// vector's elements to a larger allocation. 20:01:44 [INFO] syntax node: "/// Moves `src` into the referenced `dest`, returning the previous `dest` value.\n///\n/// Neither value is dropped.\n///\n/// * If you want to replace the values of two variables, see [`swap`].\n/// * If you want to replace with a default value, see [`take`].\n///\n/// # Examples\n///\n/// A simple example:\n///\n/// ```\n/// use std::mem;\n///\n/// let mut v: Vec<i32> = vec![1, 2];\n///\n/// let old_v = mem::replace(&mut v, vec![3, 4, 5]);\n/// assert_eq!(vec![1, 2], old_v);\n/// assert_eq!(vec![3, 4, 5], v);\n/// ```\n///\n/// `replace` allows consumption of a struct field by replacing it with another value.\n/// Without `replace` you can run into issues like these:\n///\n/// ```compile_fail,E0507\n/// struct Buffer<T> { buf: Vec<T> }\n///\n/// impl<T> Buffer<T> {\n///     fn replace_index(&mut self, i: usize, v: T) -> T {\n///         // error: cannot move out of dereference of `&mut`-pointer\n///         let t = self.buf[i];\n///         self.buf[i] = v;\n///         t\n///     }\n/// }\n/// ```\n///\n/// Note that `T` does not necessarily implement [`Clone`], so we can't even clone `self.buf[i]` to\n/// avoid the move. But `replace` can be used to disassociate the original value at that index from\n/// `self`, allowing it to be returned:\n///\n/// ```\n/// # #![allow(dead_code)]\n/// use std::mem;\n///\n/// # struct Buffer<T> { buf: Vec<T> }\n/// impl<T> Buffer<T> {\n///     fn replace_index(&mut self, i: usize, v: T) -> T {\n///         mem::replace(&mut self.buf[i], v)\n///     }\n/// }\n///\n/// let mut buffer = Buffer { buf: vec![0, 1] };\n/// assert_eq!(buffer.buf[0], 0);\n///\n/// assert_eq!(buffer.replace_index(0, 2), 0);\n/// assert_eq!(buffer.buf[0], 2);\n/// ```\n#[inline]\n#[stable(feature = \"rust1\", since = \"1.0.0\")]\n#[must_use = \"if you don't need the old value, you can just assign the new value directly\"]\n#[rustc_const_stable(feature = \"const_replace\", since = \"1.83.0\")]\n#[rustc_diagnostic_item = \"mem_replace\"]\npub const fn replace<T>(dest: &mut T, src: T) -> T {\n    // It may be tempting to use `swap` to avoid `unsafe` here. Don't!\n    // The compiler optimizes the implementation below to two `memcpy`s\n    // while `swap` would require at least three. See PR#83022 for details.\n\n    // SAFETY: We read from `dest` but directly write `src` into it afterwards,\n    // such that the old value is not duplicated. Nothing is dropped and\n    // nothing here can panic.\n    unsafe {\n        // Ideally we wouldn't use the intrinsics here, but going through the\n        // `ptr` methods introduces two unnecessary UbChecks, so until we can\n        // remove those for pointers that come from references, this uses the\n        // intrinsics instead so this stays very cheap in MIR (and debug).\n\n        let result = crate::intrinsics::read_via_copy(dest);\n        crate::intrinsics::write_via_move(dest, src);\n        result\n    }\n}"

See PR#83022 for details.\n\n    // SAFETY: We read from `dest` but directly write `src` into it afterwards,\n    // such that the old value is not duplicated. Nothing is dropped and\n    // nothing here can panic.\n    unsafe {\n        // Ideally we wouldn't use the intrinsics here, but going through the\n        // `ptr` methods introduces two unnecessary UbChecks, so until we can\n        // remove those for pointers that come from references, this uses the\n        // intrinsics instead so this stays very cheap in MIR (and debug).\n\n        let result = crate::intrinsics::read_via_copy(dest);\n        crate::intrinsics::write_via_move(dest, src);\n        result\n    }\n}"

If the tag matches `self`, returns\n    /// whether the value is constructed.\n    pub fn take_from_if<S: Source>(\n        self,\n        source: &mut S,\n    ) -> Result<Option<bool>, DecodeError<S::Error>> {\n        if source.request(1)? == 0 {\n            return Ok(None)\n        }\n        let byte = source.slice()[0];\n        // clear constructed bit\n        let mut data = [byte & !Tag::CONSTRUCTED_MASK, 0, 0, 0];\n        if (data[0] & Tag::SINGLEBYTE_DATA_MASK) == Tag::SINGLEBYTE_DATA_MASK {\n            let mut i = 1;\n            loop {\n                if source.request(i + 1)? == 0 {\n                    // Not enough data for a complete tag.\n                    return Err(source.content_err(\"short tag value\"))\n                }\n                data[i] = source.slice()[i];\n                if data[i] & Tag::LAST_OCTET_MASK == 0 {\n                    break\n                }\n                // We don’t support tags larger than 4 bytes.\n                if i == 3 {\n                    return Err(source.content_err(\n                        \"tag values longer than 4 bytes not implemented\"\n                    ))\n                }\n                i += 1;\n            }\n        }\n        let (tag, compressed) = (Tag(data), byte & Tag::CONSTRUCTED_MASK != 0);\n        if tag == self {\n            source.advance(tag.encoded_len());\n            Ok(Some(compressed))\n        }\n        else {\n            Ok(None)\n        }\n    }"

as usize) << 8 |\n                    (source.take_u8()? as usize);\n                if mode.is_ber() || len > 255 {\n                    Ok(Length::Definite(len))\n                }\n                else {\n                    Err(source.content_err(\"invalid length\"))\n                }\n            }\n            0x83 => {\n                let len =\n                    (source.take_u8()? 20:01:45 [INFO] FUNCTION: "/// Skips over content.\n    pub fn skip_opt<F>(\n        &mut self, mut op: F,\n    ) -> Result<Option<()>, DecodeError<S::Error>>\n    where F: FnMut(Tag, bool, usize) -> Result<(), ContentError> {\n        // If we already know we are at the end of the value, we can return.\n        if self.is_exhausted() {\n            return Ok(None)\n        }\n\n        // The stack for unrolling the recursion. For each level, we keep the\n        // limit the source should be set to when the value ends. For\n        // indefinite values, we keep `None`.\n        let mut stack = SmallVec::<[Option<Option<usize>>; 4]>::new();\n\n        loop {\n            // Get a the ‘header’ of a value.\n            let (tag, constructed) = Tag::take_from(self.source)?;\n            let length = Length::take_from(self.source, self.mode)?;\n\n            if !constructed {\n                if tag == Tag::END_OF_VALUE {\n                    if length != Length::Definite(0) {\n                        return Err(self.content_err(\"non-empty end of value\"))\n                    }\n\n                    // End-of-value: The top of the stack needs to be an\n                    // indefinite value for it to be allowed. If it is, pop\n                    // that value off the stack and continue. The limit is\n                    // still that from the value one level above.\n                    match stack.pop() {\n                        Some(None) => { }\n                        None => {\n                            // We read end-of-value as the very first value.\n                            // This can only happen if the outer value is\n                            // an indefinite value. If so, change state and\n                            // return.\n                            if self.state == State::Indefinite {\n                                self.state = State::Done;\n                                return Ok(None)\n                            }\n                            else {\n                                return Err(self.content_err(\n                                    \"invalid nested values\"\n                                ))\n                            }\n                        }\n                        _ => {\n                            return Err(self.content_err(\n                                \"invalid nested values\"\n                            ))\n                        }\n                    }\n                }\n                else {\n                    // Primitive value. Check for the length to be definite,\n                    // check that the caller likes it, then try to read over\n                    // it.\n                    if let Length::Definite(len) = length {\n                        if let Err(err) = op(tag, constructed, stack.len()) {\n                            return Err(self.content_err(err));\n                        }\n                        self.source.advance(len);\n                    }\n                    else {\n                        return Err(self.content_err(\n                            \"primitive value with indefinite length\"\n                        ))\n                    }\n                }\n            }\n            else if let Length::Definite(len) = length {\n                // Definite constructed value. First check if the caller\n                // likes it. Check that there is enough limit left for the\n                // value. If so, push the limit at the end of the value to\n                // the stack, update the limit to our length, and continue.\n                if let Err(err) = op(tag, constructed, stack.len()) {\n                    return Err(self.content_err(err));\n                }\n                stack.push(Some(match self.source.limit() {\n                    Some(limit) => {\n                        match limit.checked_sub(len) {\n                            Some(len) => Some(len),\n                            None => {\n                                return Err(self.content_err(\n                                    \"invalid nested values\"\n                                ));\n                            }\n                        }\n                    }\n                    None => None,\n                }));\n                self.source.set_limit(Some(len));\n            }\n            else {\n                // Indefinite constructed value. Simply push a `None` to the\n                // stack, if the caller likes it.\n                if let Err(err) = op(tag, constructed, stack.len()) {\n                    return Err(self.content_err(err));\n                }\n                stack.push(None);\n                continue;\n            }\n\n            // Now we need to check if we have reached the end of a\n            // constructed value. This happens if the limit of the\n            // source reaches 0. Since the ends of several stacked values\n            // can align, we need to loop here. 20:01:45 [INFO] syntax node: "/// Skips over content.\n    pub fn skip_opt<F>(\n        &mut self, mut op: F,\n    ) -> Result<Option<()>, DecodeError<S::Error>>\n    where F: FnMut(Tag, bool, usize) -> Result<(), ContentError> {\n        // If we already know we are at the end of the value, we can return.\n        if self.is_exhausted() {\n            return Ok(None)\n        }\n\n        // The stack for unrolling the recursion. For each level, we keep the\n        // limit the source should be set to when the value ends. For\n        // indefinite values, we keep `None`.\n        let mut stack = SmallVec::<[Option<Option<usize>>; 4]>::new();\n\n        loop {\n            // Get a the ‘header’ of a value.\n            let (tag, constructed) = Tag::take_from(self.source)?;\n            let length = Length::take_from(self.source, self.mode)?;\n\n            if !constructed {\n                if tag == Tag::END_OF_VALUE {\n                    if length != Length::Definite(0) {\n                        return Err(self.content_err(\"non-empty end of value\"))\n                    }\n\n                    // End-of-value: The top of the stack needs to be an\n                    // indefinite value for it to be allowed. If it is, pop\n                    // that value off the stack and continue. The limit is\n                    // still that from the value one level above.\n                    match stack.pop() {\n                        Some(None) => { }\n                        None => {\n                            // We read end-of-value as the very first value.\n                            // This can only happen if the outer value is\n                            // an indefinite value. If so, change state and\n                            // return.\n                            if self.state == State::Indefinite {\n                                self.state = State::Done;\n                                return Ok(None)\n                            }\n                            else {\n                                return Err(self.content_err(\n                                    \"invalid nested values\"\n                                ))\n                            }\n                        }\n                        _ => {\n                            return Err(self.content_err(\n                                \"invalid nested values\"\n                            ))\n                        }\n                    }\n                }\n                else {\n                    // Primitive value. Check for the length to be definite,\n                    // check that the caller likes it, then try to read over\n                    // it.\n                    if let Length::Definite(len) = length {\n                        if let Err(err) = op(tag, constructed, stack.len()) {\n                            return Err(self.content_err(err));\n                        }\n                        self.source.advance(len);\n                    }\n                    else {\n                        return Err(self.content_err(\n                            \"primitive value with indefinite length\"\n                        ))\n                    }\n                }\n            }\n            else if let Length::Definite(len) = length {\n                // Definite constructed value. First check if the caller\n                // likes it. Check that there is enough limit left for the\n                // value. If so, push the limit at the end of the value to\n                // the stack, update the limit to our length, and continue.\n                if let Err(err) = op(tag, constructed, stack.len()) {\n                    return Err(self.content_err(err));\n                }\n                stack.push(Some(match self.source.limit() {\n                    Some(limit) => {\n                        match limit.checked_sub(len) {\n                            Some(len) => Some(len),\n                            None => {\n                                return Err(self.content_err(\n                                    \"invalid nested values\"\n                                ));\n                            }\n                        }\n                    }\n                    None => None,\n                }));\n                self.source.set_limit(Some(len));\n            }\n            else {\n                // Indefinite constructed value. Simply push a `None` to the\n                // stack, if the caller likes it.\n                if let Err(err) = op(tag, constructed, stack.len()) {\n                    return Err(self.content_err(err));\n                }\n                stack.push(None);\n                continue;\n            }\n\n            // Now we need to check if we have reached the end of a\n            // constructed value. This happens if the limit of the\n            // source reaches 0. Since the ends of several stacked values\n            // can align, we need to loop here. Also, if we run out of\n            // stack, we are done.\n            loop {\n                if stack.is_empty() {\n                    return Ok(Some(()))\n                }\n                else if self.source.limit() == Some(0) {\n                    match stack.pop() {\n                        Some(Some(limit)) => {\n                            self.source.set_limit(limit)\n                        }\n                        Some(None) => {\n                            // We need a End-of-value, so running out of\n                            // data is an error.\n                            return Err(self.content_err(\"\n                                missing further values\"\n                            ))\n                        }\n                        None => unreachable!(),\n                    }\n                }\n                else {\n                    break;\n                }\n            }\n\n        }\n    }"

20:01:45 [INFO] FUNCTION: "/// Skips over content.\n    pub fn skip_opt<F>(\n        &mut self, mut op: F,\n    ) -> Result<Option<()>, DecodeError<S::Error>>\n    where F: FnMut(Tag, bool, usize) -> Result<(), ContentError> {\n        // If we already know we are at the end of the value, we can return.\n        if self.is_exhausted() {\n            return Ok(None)\n        }\n\n        // The stack for unrolling the recursion. For each level, we keep the\n        // limit the source should be set to when the value ends. For\n        // indefinite values, we keep `None`.\n        let mut stack = SmallVec::<[Option<Option<usize>>; 4]>::new();\n\n        loop {\n            // Get a the ‘header’ of a value.\n            let (tag, constructed) = Tag::take_from(self.source)?;\n            let length = Length::take_from(self.source, self.mode)?;\n\n            if !constructed {\n                if tag == Tag::END_OF_VALUE {\n                    if length != Length::Definite(0) {\n                        return Err(self.content_err(\"non-empty end of value\"))\n                    }\n\n                    // End-of-value: The top of the stack needs to be an\n                    // indefinite value for it to be allowed. If it is, pop\n                    // that value off the stack and continue. The limit is\n                    // still that from the value one level above.\n                    match stack.pop() {\n                        Some(None) => { }\n                        None => {\n                            // We read end-of-value as the very first value.\n                            // This can only happen if the outer value is\n                            // an indefinite value. If so, change state and\n                            // return.\n                            if self.state == State::Indefinite {\n                                self.state = State::Done;\n                                return Ok(None)\n                            }\n                            else {\n                                return Err(self.content_err(\n                                    \"invalid nested values\"\n                                ))\n                            }\n                        }\n                        _ => {\n                            return Err(self.content_err(\n                                \"invalid nested values\"\n                            ))\n                        }\n                    }\n                }\n                else {\n                    // Primitive value. Check for the length to be definite,\n                    // check that the caller likes it, then try to read over\n                    // it.\n                    if let Length::Definite(len) = length {\n                        if let Err(err) = op(tag, constructed, stack.len()) {\n                            return Err(self.content_err(err));\n                        }\n                        self.source.advance(len);\n                    }\n                    else {\n                        return Err(self.content_err(\n                            \"primitive value with indefinite length\"\n                        ))\n                    }\n                }\n            }\n            else if let Length::Definite(len) = length {\n                // Definite constructed value. First check if the caller\n                // likes it. Check that there is enough limit left for the\n                // value. If so, push the limit at the end of the value to\n                // the stack, update the limit to our length, and continue.\n                if let Err(err) = op(tag, constructed, stack.len()) {\n                    return Err(self.content_err(err));\n                }\n                stack.push(Some(match self.source.limit() {\n                    Some(limit) => {\n                        match limit.checked_sub(len) {\n                            Some(len) => Some(len),\n                            None => {\n                                return Err(self.content_err(\n                                    \"invalid nested values\"\n                                ));\n                            }\n                        }\n                    }\n                    None => None,\n                }));\n                self.source.set_limit(Some(len));\n            }\n            else {\n                // Indefinite constructed value. Simply push a `None` to the\n                // stack, if the caller likes it.\n                if let Err(err) = op(tag, constructed, stack.len()) {\n                    return Err(self.content_err(err));\n                }\n                stack.push(None);\n                continue;\n            }\n\n            // Now we need to check if we have reached the end of a\n            // constructed value. This happens if the limit of the\n            // source reaches 0. Since the ends of several stacked values\n            // can align, we need to loop here. Also, if we run out of\n            // stack, we are done.\n            loop {\n                if stack.is_empty() {\n                    return Ok(Some(()))\n                }\n                else if self.source.limit() == Some(0) {\n                    match stack.pop() {\n                        Some(Some(limit)) => {\n                            self.source.set_limit(limit)\n                        }\n                        Some(None) => {\n                            // We need a End-of-value, so running out of\n                            // data is an error.\n                            return Err(self.content_err(\"\n                                missing further values\"\n                            ))\n                        }\n                        None => unreachable!(),\n                    }\n                }\n                else {\n                    break;\n                }\n            }\n\n        }\n    }"

20:01:45 [INFO] syntax node: "/// Skips over content.\n    pub fn skip_opt<F>(\n        &mut self, mut op: F,\n    ) -> Result<Option<()>, DecodeError<S::Error>>\n    where F: FnMut(Tag, bool, usize) -> Result<(), ContentError> {\n        // If we already know we are at the end of the value, we can return.\n        if self.is_exhausted() {\n            return Ok(None)\n        }\n\n        // The stack for unrolling the recursion. For each level, we keep the\n        // limit the source should be set to when the value ends. For\n        // indefinite values, we keep `None`.\n        let mut stack = SmallVec::<[Option<Option<usize>>; 4]>::new();\n\n        loop {\n            // Get a the ‘header’ of a value.\n            let (tag, constructed) = Tag::take_from(self.source)?;\n            let length = Length::take_from(self.source, self.mode)?;\n\n            if !constructed {\n                if tag == Tag::END_OF_VALUE {\n                    if length != Length::Definite(0) {\n                        return Err(self.content_err(\"non-empty end of value\"))\n                    }\n\n                    // End-of-value: The top of the stack needs to be an\n                    // indefinite value for it to be allowed. If it is, pop\n                    // that value off the stack and continue. The limit is\n                    // still that from the value one level above.\n                    match stack.pop() {\n                        Some(None) => { }\n                        None => {\n                            // We read end-of-value as the very first value.\n                            // This can only happen if the outer value is\n                            // an indefinite value. If so, change state and\n                            // return.\n                            if self.state == State::Indefinite {\n                                self.state = State::Done;\n                                return Ok(None)\n                            }\n                            else {\n                                return Err(self.content_err(\n                                    \"invalid nested values\"\n                                ))\n                            }\n                        }\n                        _ => {\n                            return Err(self.content_err(\n                                \"invalid nested values\"\n                            ))\n                        }\n                    }\n                }\n                else {\n                    // Primitive value. Check for the length to be definite,\n                    // check that the caller likes it, then try to read over\n                    // it.\n                    if let Length::Definite(len) = length {\n                        if let Err(err) = op(tag, constructed, stack.len()) {\n                            return Err(self.content_err(err));\n                        }\n                        self.source.advance(len);\n                    }\n                    else {\n                        return Err(self.content_err(\n                            \"primitive value with indefinite length\"\n                        ))\n                    }\n                }\n            }\n            else if let Length::Definite(len) = length {\n                // Definite constructed value. First check if the caller\n                // likes it. Check that there is enough limit left for the\n                // value. If so, push the limit at the end of the value to\n                // the stack, update the limit to our length, and continue.\n                if let Err(err) = op(tag, constructed, stack.len()) {\n                    return Err(self.content_err(err));\n                }\n                stack.push(Some(match self.source.limit() {\n                    Some(limit) => {\n                        match limit.checked_sub(len) {\n                            Some(len) => Some(len),\n                            None => {\n                                return Err(self.content_err(\n                                    \"invalid nested values\"\n                                ));\n                            }\n                        }\n                    }\n                    None => None,\n                }));\n                self.source.set_limit(Some(len));\n            }\n            else {\n                // Indefinite constructed value. Simply push a `None` to the\n                // stack, if the caller likes it.\n                if let Err(err) = op(tag, constructed, stack.len()) {\n                    return Err(self.content_err(err));\n                }\n                stack.push(None);\n                continue;\n            }\n\n            // Now we need to check if we have reached the end of a\n            // constructed value. This happens if the limit of the\n            // source reaches 0. Since the ends of several stacked values\n            // can align, we need to loop here. Also, if we run out of\n            // stack, we are done.\n            loop {\n                if stack.is_empty() {\n                    return Ok(Some(()))\n                }\n                else if self.source.limit() == Some(0) {\n                    match stack.pop() {\n                        Some(Some(limit)) => {\n                            self.source.set_limit(limit)\n                        }\n                        Some(None) => {\n                            // We need a End-of-value, so running out of\n                            // data is an error.\n                            return Err(self.content_err(\"\n                                missing further values\"\n                            ))\n                        }\n                        None => unreachable!(),\n                    }\n                }\n                else {\n                    break;\n                }\n            }\n\n        }\n    }"

20:01:45 [INFO] syntax node: "/// Moves `src` into the referenced `dest`, returning the previous `dest` value.\n///\n/// Neither value is dropped.\n///\n/// * If you want to replace the values of two variables, see [`swap`].\n/// * If you want to replace with a default value, see [`take`].\n///\n/// # Examples\n///\n/// A simple example:\n///\n/// ```\n/// use std::mem;\n///\n/// let mut v: Vec<i32> = vec![1, 2];\n///\n/// let old_v = mem::replace(&mut v, vec![3, 4, 5]);\n/// assert_eq!(vec![1, 2], old_v);\n/// assert_eq!(vec![3, 4, 5], v);\n/// ```\n///\n/// `replace` allows consumption of a struct field by replacing it with another value.\n/// Without `replace` you can run into issues like these:\n///\n/// ```compile_fail,E0507\n/// struct Buffer<T> { buf: Vec<T> }\n///\n/// impl<T> Buffer<T> {\n///     fn replace_index(&mut self, i: usize, v: T) -> T {\n///         // error: cannot move out of dereference of `&mut`-pointer\n///         let t = self.buf[i];\n///         self.buf[i] = v;\n///         t\n///     }\n/// }\n/// ```\n///\n/// Note that `T` does not necessarily implement [`Clone`], so we can't even clone `self.buf[i]` to\n/// avoid the move. But `replace` can be used to disassociate the original value at that index from\n/// `self`, allowing it to be returned:\n///\n/// ```\n/// # #![allow(dead_code)]\n/// use std::mem;\n///\n/// # struct Buffer<T> { buf: Vec<T> }\n/// impl<T> Buffer<T> {\n///     fn replace_index(&mut self, i: usize, v: T) -> T {\n///         mem::replace(&mut self.buf[i], v)\n///     }\n/// }\n///\n/// let mut buffer = Buffer { buf: vec![0, 1] };\n/// assert_eq!(buffer.buf[0], 0);\n///\n/// assert_eq!(buffer.replace_index(0, 2), 0);\n/// assert_eq!(buffer.buf[0], 2);\n/// ```\n#[inline]\n#[stable(feature = \"rust1\", since = \"1.0.0\")]\n#[must_use = \"if you don't need the old value, you can just assign the new value directly\"]\n#[rustc_const_stable(feature = \"const_replace\", since = \"1.83.0\")]\n#[rustc_diagnostic_item = \"mem_replace\"]\npub const fn replace<T>(dest: &mut T, src: T) -> T {\n    // It may be tempting to use `swap` to avoid `unsafe` here. Don't!\n    // The compiler optimizes the implementation below to two `memcpy`s\n    // while `swap` would require at least three. See PR#83022 for details.\n\n    // SAFETY: We read from `dest` but directly write `src` into it afterwards,\n    // such that the old value is not duplicated. Nothing is dropped and\n    // nothing here can panic.\n    unsafe {\n        // Ideally we wouldn't use the intrinsics here, but going through the\n        // `ptr` methods introduces two unnecessary UbChecks, so until we can\n        // remove those for pointers that come from references, this uses the\n        // intrinsics instead so this stays very cheap in MIR (and debug).\n\n        let result = crate::intrinsics::read_via_copy(dest);\n        crate::intrinsics::write_via_move(dest, src);\n        result\n    }\n}"

20:01:45 [INFO] syntax node: "/// Moves `src` into the referenced `dest`, returning the previous `dest` value.\n///\n/// Neither value is dropped.\n///\n/// * If you want to replace the values of two variables, see [`swap`].\n/// * If you want to replace with a default value, see [`take`].\n///\n/// # Examples\n///\n/// A simple example:\n///\n/// ```\n/// use std::mem;\n///\n/// let mut v: Vec<i32> = vec![1, 2];\n///\n/// let old_v = mem::replace(&mut v, vec![3, 4, 5]);\n/// assert_eq!(vec![1, 2], old_v);\n/// assert_eq!(vec![3, 4, 5], v);\n/// ```\n///\n/// `replace` allows consumption of a struct field by replacing it with another value.\n/// Without `replace` you can run into issues like these:\n///\n/// ```compile_fail,E0507\n/// struct Buffer<T> { buf: Vec<T> }\n///\n/// impl<T> Buffer<T> {\n///     fn replace_index(&mut self, i: usize, v: T) -> T {\n///         // error: cannot move out of dereference of `&mut`-pointer\n///         let t = self.buf[i];\n///         self.buf[i] = v;\n///         t\n///     }\n/// }\n/// ```\n///\n/// Note that `T` does not necessarily implement [`Clone`], so we can't even clone `self.buf[i]` to\n/// avoid the move. But `replace` can be used to disassociate the original value at that index from\n/// `self`, allowing it to be returned:\n///\n/// ```\n/// # #![allow(dead_code)]\n/// use std::mem;\n///\n/// # struct Buffer<T> { buf: Vec<T> }\n/// impl<T> Buffer<T> {\n///     fn replace_index(&mut self, i: usize, v: T) -> T {\n///         mem::replace(&mut self.buf[i], v)\n///     }\n/// }\n///\n/// let mut buffer = Buffer { buf: vec![0, 1] };\n/// assert_eq!(buffer.buf[0], 0);\n///\n/// assert_eq!(buffer.replace_index(0, 2), 0);\n/// assert_eq!(buffer.buf[0], 2);\n/// ```\n#[inline]\n#[stable(feature = \"rust1\", since = \"1.0.0\")]\n#[must_use = \"if you don't need the old value, you can just assign the new value directly\"]\n#[rustc_const_stable(feature = \"const_replace\", since = \"1.83.0\")]\n#[rustc_diagnostic_item = \"mem_replace\"]\npub const fn replace<T>(dest: &mut T, src: T) -> T {\n    // It may be tempting to use `swap` to avoid `unsafe` here. Don't!\n    // The compiler optimizes the implementation below to two `memcpy`s\n    // while `swap` would require at least three. See PR#83022 for details.\n\n    // SAFETY: We read from `dest` but directly write `src` into it afterwards,\n    // such that the old value is not duplicated. Nothing is dropped and\n    // nothing here can panic.\n    unsafe {\n        // Ideally we wouldn't use the intrinsics here, but going through the\n        // `ptr` methods introduces two unnecessary UbChecks, so until we can\n        // remove those for pointers that come from references, this uses the\n        // intrinsics instead so this stays very cheap in MIR (and debug).\n\n        let result = crate::intrinsics::read_via_copy(dest);\n        crate::intrinsics::write_via_move(dest, src);\n        result\n    }\n}"

20:01:45 [INFO] syntax node: "/// Folds every element into an accumulator by applying an operation,\n    /// returning the final result.\n    ///\n    /// `fold()` takes two arguments: an initial value, and a closure with two\n    /// arguments: an 'accumulator', and an element. The closure returns the value that\n    /// the accumulator should have for the next iteration.\n    ///\n    /// The initial value is the value the accumulator will have on the first\n    /// call.\n    ///\n    /// After applying this closure to every element of the iterator, `fold()`\n    /// returns the accumulator.\n    ///\n    /// This operation is sometimes called 'reduce' or 'inject'.\n    ///\n    /// Folding is useful whenever you have a collection of something, and want\n    /// to produce a single value from it.\n    ///\n    /// Note: `fold()`, and similar methods that traverse the entire iterator,\n    /// might not terminate for infinite iterators, even on traits for which a\n    /// result is determinable in finite time.\n    ///\n    /// Note: [`reduce()`] can be used to use the first element as the initial\n    /// value, if the accumulator type and item type is the same.\n    ///\n    /// Note: `fold()` combines elements in a *left-associative* fashion. For associative\n    /// operators like `+`, the order the elements are combined in is not important, but for non-associative\n    /// operators like `-` the order will affect the final result.\n    /// For a *right-associative* version of `fold()`, see [`DoubleEndedIterator::rfold()`].\n    ///\n    /// # Note to Implementors\n    ///\n    /// Several of the other (forward) methods have default implementations in\n    /// terms of this one, so try to implement this explicitly if it can\n    /// do something better than the default `for` loop implementation.\n    ///\n    /// In particular, try to have this call `fold()` on the internal parts\n    /// from which this iterator is composed.\n    ///\n    /// # Examples\n    ///\n    /// Basic usage:\n    ///\n    /// ```\n    /// let a = [1, 2, 3];\n    ///\n    /// // the sum of all of the elements of the array\n    /// let sum = a.iter().fold(0, |acc, x| acc + x);\n    ///\n    /// assert_eq!(sum, 6);\n    /// ```\n    ///\n    /// Let's walk through each step of the iteration here:\n    ///\n    /// | element | acc | x | result |\n    /// |---------|-----|---|--------|\n    /// |         | 0   |   |        |\n    /// | 1       | 0   | 1 | 1      |\n    /// | 2       | 1   | 2 | 3      |\n    /// | 3       | 3   | 3 | 6      |\n    ///\n    /// And so, our final result, `6`.\n    ///\n    /// This example demonstrates the left-associative nature of `fold()`:\n    /// it builds a string, starting with an initial value\n    /// and continuing with each element from the front until the back:\n    ///\n    /// ```\n    /// let numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];\n    ///\n    /// let zero = \"0\".to_string();\n    ///\n    /// let result = numbers.iter().fold(zero, |acc, &x| {\n    ///     format!(\"({acc} + {x})\")\n    /// });\n    ///\n    /// assert_eq!(result, \"(((((0 + 1) + 2) + 3) + 4) + 5)\");\n    /// ```\n    /// It's common for people who haven't used iterators a lot to\n    /// use a `for` loop with a list of things to build up a result. Those\n    /// can be turned into `fold()`s:\n    ///\n    /// [`for`]: ../../book/ch03-05-control-flow.html#looping-through-a-collection-with-for\n    ///\n    /// ```\n    /// let numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];\n    ///\n    /// let mut result = 0;\n    ///\n    /// // for loop:\n    /// for i in &numbers {\n    ///     result = result + i;\n    /// }\n    ///\n    /// // fold:\n    /// let result2 = numbers.iter().fold(0, |acc, &x| acc + x);\n    ///\n    /// // they're the same\n    /// assert_eq!(result, result2);\n    /// ```\n    ///\n    /// [`reduce()`]: Iterator::reduce\n    #[doc(alias = \"inject\", alias = \"foldl\")]\n    #[inline]\n    #[stable(feature = \"rust1\", since = \"1.0.0\")]\n    fn fold<B, F>(mut self, init: B, mut f: F) -> B\n    where\n        Self: Sized,\n        F: FnMut(B, Self::Item) -> B,\n    {\n        let mut accum = init;\n        while let Some(x) = self.next() {\n            accum = f(accum, x);\n        }\n        accum\n    }"

20:01:45 [INFO] syntax node: "/// Folds every element into an accumulator by applying an operation,\n    /// returning the final result.\n    ///\n    /// `fold()` takes two arguments: an initial value, and a closure with two\n    /// arguments: an 'accumulator', and an element. The closure returns the value that\n    /// the accumulator should have for the next iteration.\n    ///\n    /// The initial value is the value the accumulator will have on the first\n    /// call.\n    ///\n    /// After applying this closure to every element of the iterator, `fold()`\n    /// returns the accumulator.\n    ///\n    /// This operation is sometimes called 'reduce' or 'inject'.\n    ///\n    /// Folding is useful whenever you have a collection of something, and want\n    /// to produce a single value from it.\n    ///\n    /// Note: `fold()`, and similar methods that traverse the entire iterator,\n    /// might not terminate for infinite iterators, even on traits for which a\n    /// result is determinable in finite time.\n    ///\n    /// Note: [`reduce()`] can be used to use the first element as the initial\n    /// value, if the accumulator type and item type is the same.\n    ///\n    /// Note: `fold()` combines elements in a *left-associative* fashion. For associative\n    /// operators like `+`, the order the elements are combined in is not important, but for non-associative\n    /// operators like `-` the order will affect the final result.\n    /// For a *right-associative* version of `fold()`, see [`DoubleEndedIterator::rfold()`].\n    ///\n    /// # Note to Implementors\n    ///\n    /// Several of the other (forward) methods have default implementations in\n    /// terms of this one, so try to implement this explicitly if it can\n    /// do something better than the default `for` loop implementation.\n    ///\n    /// In particular, try to have this call `fold()` on the internal parts\n    /// from which this iterator is composed.\n    ///\n    /// # Examples\n    ///\n    /// Basic usage:\n    ///\n    /// ```\n    /// let a = [1, 2, 3];\n    ///\n    /// // the sum of all of the elements of the array\n    /// let sum = a.iter().fold(0, |acc, x| acc + x);\n    ///\n    /// assert_eq!(sum, 6);\n    /// ```\n    ///\n    /// Let's walk through each step of the iteration here:\n    ///\n    /// | element | acc | x | result |\n    /// |---------|-----|---|--------|\n    /// |         | 0   |   |        |\n    /// | 1       | 0   | 1 | 1      |\n    /// | 2       | 1   | 2 | 3      |\n    /// | 3       | 3   | 3 | 6      |\n    ///\n    /// And so, our final result, `6`.\n    ///\n    /// This example demonstrates the left-associative nature of `fold()`:\n    /// it builds a string, starting with an initial value\n    /// and continuing with each element from the front until the back:\n    ///\n    /// ```\n    /// let numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];\n    ///\n    /// let zero = \"0\".to_string();\n    ///\n    /// let result = numbers.iter().fold(zero, |acc, &x| {\n    ///     format!(\"({acc} + {x})\")\n    /// });\n    ///\n    /// assert_eq!(result, \"(((((0 + 1) + 2) + 3) + 4) + 5)\");\n    /// ```\n    /// It's common for people who haven't used iterators a lot to\n    /// use a `for` loop with a list of things to build up a result. Those\n    /// can be turned into `fold()`s:\n    ///\n    /// [`for`]: ../../book/ch03-05-control-flow.html#looping-through-a-collection-with-for\n    ///\n    /// ```\n    /// let numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];\n    ///\n    /// let mut result = 0;\n    ///\n    /// // for loop:\n    /// for i in &numbers {\n    ///     result = result + i;\n    /// }\n    ///\n    /// // fold:\n    /// let result2 = numbers.iter().fold(0, |acc, &x| acc + x);\n    ///\n    /// // they're the same\n    /// assert_eq!(result, result2);\n    /// ```\n    ///\n    /// [`reduce()`]: Iterator::reduce\n    #[doc(alias = \"inject\", alias = \"foldl\")]\n    #[inline]\n    #[stable(feature = \"rust1\", since = \"1.0.0\")]\n    fn fold<B, F>(mut self, init: B, mut f: F) -> B\n    where\n        Self: Sized,\n        F: FnMut(B, Self::Item) -> B,\n    {\n        let mut accum = init;\n        while let Some(x) = self.next() {\n            accum = f(accum, x);\n        }\n        accum\n    }"

20:01:45 [INFO] syntax node: "/// Skips over content.\n    pub fn skip_opt<F>(\n        &mut self, mut op: F,\n    ) -> Result<Option<()>, DecodeError<S::Error>>\n    where F: FnMut(Tag, bool, usize) -> Result<(), ContentError> {\n        // If we already know we are at the end of the value, we can return.\n        if self.is_exhausted() {\n            return Ok(None)\n        }\n\n        // The stack for unrolling the recursion. For each level, we keep the\n        // limit the source should be set to when the value ends. For\n        // indefinite values, we keep `None`.\n        let mut stack = SmallVec::<[Option<Option<usize>>; 4]>::new();\n\n        loop {\n            // Get a the ‘header’ of a value.\n            let (tag, constructed) = Tag::take_from(self.source)?;\n            let length = Length::take_from(self.source, self.mode)?;\n\n            if !constructed {\n                if tag == Tag::END_OF_VALUE {\n                    if length != Length::Definite(0) {\n                        return Err(self.content_err(\"non-empty end of value\"))\n                    }\n\n                    // End-of-value: The top of the stack needs to be an\n                    // indefinite value for it to be allowed. If it is, pop\n                    // that value off the stack and continue. The limit is\n                    // still that from the value one level above.\n                    match stack.pop() {\n                        Some(None) => { }\n                        None => {\n                            // We read end-of-value as the very first value.\n                            // This can only happen if the outer value is\n                            // an indefinite value. If so, change state and\n                            // return.\n                            if self.state == State::Indefinite {\n                                self.state = State::Done;\n                                return Ok(None)\n                            }\n                            else {\n                                return Err(self.content_err(\n                                    \"invalid nested values\"\n                                ))\n                            }\n                        }\n                        _ => {\n                            return Err(self.content_err(\n                                \"invalid nested values\"\n                            ))\n                        }\n                    }\n                }\n                else {\n                    // Primitive value. Check for the length to be definite,\n                    // check that the caller likes it, then try to read over\n                    // it.\n                    if let Length::Definite(len) = length {\n                        if let Err(err) = op(tag, constructed, stack.len()) {\n                            return Err(self.content_err(err));\n                        }\n                        self.source.advance(len);\n                    }\n                    else {\n                        return Err(self.content_err(\n                            \"primitive value with indefinite length\"\n                        ))\n                    }\n                }\n            }\n            else if let Length::Definite(len) = length {\n                // Definite constructed value. First check if the caller\n                // likes it. Check that there is enough limit left for the\n                // value. If so, push the limit at the end of the value to\n                // the stack, update the limit to our length, and continue.\n                if let Err(err) = op(tag, constructed, stack.len()) {\n                    return Err(self.content_err(err));\n                }\n                stack.push(Some(match self.source.limit() {\n                    Some(limit) => {\n                        match limit.checked_sub(len) {\n                            Some(len) => Some(len),\n                            None => {\n                                return Err(self.content_err(\n                                    \"invalid nested values\"\n                                ));\n                            }\n                        }\n                    }\n                    None => None,\n                }));\n                self.source.set_limit(Some(len));\n            }\n            else {\n                // Indefinite constructed value. Simply push a `None` to the\n                // stack, if the caller likes it.\n                if let Err(err) = op(tag, constructed, stack.len()) {\n                    return Err(self.content_err(err));\n                }\n                stack.push(None);\n                continue;\n            }\n\n            // Now we need to check if we have reached the end of a\n            // constructed value. This happens if the limit of the\n            // source reaches 0. Since the ends of several stacked values\n            // can align, we need to loop here. Also, if we run out of\n            // stack, we are done.\n            loop {\n                if stack.is_empty() {\n                    return Ok(Some(()))\n                }\n                else if self.source.limit() == Some(0) {\n                    match stack.pop() {\n                        Some(Some(limit)) => {\n                            self.source.set_limit(limit)\n                        }\n                        Some(None) => {\n                            // We need a End-of-value, so running out of\n                            // data is an error.\n                            return Err(self.content_err(\"\n                                missing further values\"\n                            ))\n                        }\n                        None => unreachable!(),\n                    }\n                }\n                else {\n                    break;\n                }\n            }\n\n        }\n    }"

20:01:45 [INFO] syntax node: "/// Skips over content.\n    pub fn skip_opt<F>(\n        &mut self, mut op: F,\n    ) -> Result<Option<()>, DecodeError<S::Error>>\n    where F: FnMut(Tag, bool, usize) -> Result<(), ContentError> {\n        // If we already know we are at the end of the value, we can return.\n        if self.is_exhausted() {\n            return Ok(None)\n        }\n\n        // The stack for unrolling the recursion. For each level, we keep the\n        // limit the source should be set to when the value ends. For\n        // indefinite values, we keep `None`.\n        let mut stack = SmallVec::<[Option<Option<usize>>; 4]>::new();\n\n        loop {\n            // Get a the ‘header’ of a value.\n            let (tag, constructed) = Tag::take_from(self.source)?;\n            let length = Length::take_from(self.source, self.mode)?;\n\n            if !constructed {\n                if tag == Tag::END_OF_VALUE {\n                    if length != Length::Definite(0) {\n                        return Err(self.content_err(\"non-empty end of value\"))\n                    }\n\n                    // End-of-value: The top of the stack needs to be an\n                    // indefinite value for it to be allowed. If it is, pop\n                    // that value off the stack and continue. The limit is\n                    // still that from the value one level above.\n                    match stack.pop() {\n                        Some(None) => { }\n                        None => {\n                            // We read end-of-value as the very first value.\n                            // This can only happen if the outer value is\n                            // an indefinite value. If so, change state and\n                            // return.\n                            if self.state == State::Indefinite {\n                                self.state = State::Done;\n                                return Ok(None)\n                            }\n                            else {\n                                return Err(self.content_err(\n                                    \"invalid nested values\"\n                                ))\n                            }\n                        }\n                        _ => {\n                            return Err(self.content_err(\n                                \"invalid nested values\"\n                            ))\n                        }\n                    }\n                }\n                else {\n                    // Primitive value. Check for the length to be definite,\n                    // check that the caller likes it, then try to read over\n                    // it.\n                    if let Length::Definite(len) = length {\n                        if let Err(err) = op(tag, constructed, stack.len()) {\n                            return Err(self.content_err(err));\n                        }\n                        self.source.advance(len);\n                    }\n                    else {\n                        return Err(self.content_err(\n                            \"primitive value with indefinite length\"\n                        ))\n                    }\n                }\n            }\n            else if let Length::Definite(len) = length {\n                // Definite constructed value. First check if the caller\n                // likes it. Check that there is enough limit left for the\n                // value. If so, push the limit at the end of the value to\n                // the stack, update the limit to our length, and continue.\n                if let Err(err) = op(tag, constructed, stack.len()) {\n                    return Err(self.content_err(err));\n                }\n                stack.push(Some(match self.source.limit() {\n                    Some(limit) => {\n                        match limit.checked_sub(len) {\n                            Some(len) => Some(len),\n                            None => {\n                                return Err(self.content_err(\n                                    \"invalid nested values\"\n                                ));\n                            }\n                        }\n                    }\n                    None => None,\n                }));\n                self.source.set_limit(Some(len));\n            }\n            else {\n                // Indefinite constructed value. Simply push a `None` to the\n                // stack, if the caller likes it.\n                if let Err(err) = op(tag, constructed, stack.len()) {\n                    return Err(self.content_err(err));\n                }\n                stack.push(None);\n                continue;\n            }\n\n            // Now we need to check if we have reached the end of a\n            // constructed value. This happens if the limit of the\n            // source reaches 0. Since the ends of several stacked values\n            // can align, we need to loop here. Also, if we run out of\n            // stack, we are done.\n            loop {\n                if stack.is_empty() {\n                    return Ok(Some(()))\n                }\n                else if self.source.limit() == Some(0) {\n                    match stack.pop() {\n                        Some(Some(limit)) => {\n                            self.source.set_limit(limit)\n                        }\n                        Some(None) => {\n                            // We need a End-of-value, so running out of\n                            // data is an error.\n                            return Err(self.content_err(\"\n                                missing further values\"\n                            ))\n                        }\n                        None => unreachable!(),\n                    }\n                }\n                else {\n                    break;\n                }\n            }\n\n        }\n    }"

But `replace` can be used to disassociate the original value at that index from\n/// `self`, allowing it to be returned:\n///\n/// ```\n/// # #![allow(dead_code)]\n/// use std::mem;\n///\n/// # struct Buffer<T> { buf: Vec<T> }\n/// impl<T> Buffer<T> {\n///     fn replace_index(&mut self, i: usize, v: T) -> T {\n///         mem::replace(&mut self.buf[i], v)\n///     }\n/// }\n///\n/// let mut buffer = Buffer { buf: vec![0, 1] };\n/// assert_eq!(buffer.buf[0], 0);\n///\n/// assert_eq!(buffer.replace_index(0, 2), 0);\n/// assert_eq!(buffer.buf[0], 2);\n/// ```\n#[inline]\n#[stable(feature = \"rust1\", since = \"1.0.0\")]\n#[must_use = \"if you don't need the old value, you can just assign the new value directly\"]\n#[rustc_const_stable(feature = \"const_replace\", since = \"1.83.0\")]\n#[rustc_diagnostic_item = \"mem_replace\"]\npub const fn replace<T>(dest: &mut T, src: T) -> T {\n    // It may be tempting to use `swap` to avoid `unsafe` here. Don't!\n    // The compiler optimizes the implementation below to two `memcpy`s\n    // while `swap` would require at least three. 20:01:46 [INFO] syntax node: "/// Moves `src` into the referenced `dest`, returning the previous `dest` value.\n///\n/// Neither value is dropped.\n///\n/// * If you want to replace the values of two variables, see [`swap`].\n/// * If you want to replace with a default value, see [`take`].\n///\n/// # Examples\n///\n/// A simple example:\n///\n/// ```\n/// use std::mem;\n///\n/// let mut v: Vec<i32> = vec![1, 2];\n///\n/// let old_v = mem::replace(&mut v, vec![3, 4, 5]);\n/// assert_eq!(vec![1, 2], old_v);\n/// assert_eq!(vec![3, 4, 5], v);\n/// ```\n///\n/// `replace` allows consumption of a struct field by replacing it with another value.\n/// Without `replace` you can run into issues like these:\n///\n/// ```compile_fail,E0507\n/// struct Buffer<T> { buf: Vec<T> }\n///\n/// impl<T> Buffer<T> {\n///     fn replace_index(&mut self, i: usize, v: T) -> T {\n///         // error: cannot move out of dereference of `&mut`-pointer\n///         let t = self.buf[i];\n///         self.buf[i] = v;\n///         t\n///     }\n/// }\n/// ```\n///\n/// Note that `T` does not necessarily implement [`Clone`], so we can't even clone `self.buf[i]` to\n/// avoid the move. But `replace` can be used to disassociate the original value at that index from\n/// `self`, allowing it to be returned:\n///\n/// ```\n/// # #![allow(dead_code)]\n/// use std::mem;\n///\n/// # struct Buffer<T> { buf: Vec<T> }\n/// impl<T> Buffer<T> {\n///     fn replace_index(&mut self, i: usize, v: T) -> T {\n///         mem::replace(&mut self.buf[i], v)\n///     }\n/// }\n///\n/// let mut buffer = Buffer { buf: vec![0, 1] };\n/// assert_eq!(buffer.buf[0], 0);\n///\n/// assert_eq!(buffer.replace_index(0, 2), 0);\n/// assert_eq!(buffer.buf[0], 2);\n/// ```\n#[inline]\n#[stable(feature = \"rust1\", since = \"1.0.0\")]\n#[must_use = \"if you don't need the old value, you can just assign the new value directly\"]\n#[rustc_const_stable(feature = \"const_replace\", since = \"1.83.0\")]\n#[rustc_diagnostic_item = \"mem_replace\"]\npub const fn replace<T>(dest: &mut T, src: T) -> T {\n    // It may be tempting to use `swap` to avoid `unsafe` here. Don't!\n    // The compiler optimizes the implementation below to two `memcpy`s\n    // while `swap` would require at least three. See PR#83022 for details.\n\n    // SAFETY: We read from `dest` but directly write `src` into it afterwards,\n    // such that the old value is not duplicated. Nothing is dropped and\n    // nothing here can panic.\n    unsafe {\n        // Ideally we wouldn't use the intrinsics here, but going through the\n        // `ptr` methods introduces two unnecessary UbChecks, so until we can\n        // remove those for pointers that come from references, this uses the\n        // intrinsics instead so this stays very cheap in MIR (and debug).\n\n        let result = crate::intrinsics::read_via_copy(dest);\n        crate::intrinsics::write_via_move(dest, src);\n        result\n    }\n}"
